original.question: What does class abstraction mean?
options: Declaring every data field of the class as public
Separating how a class is implemented from how it is used
Writing a class that cannot be instantiated
Copying the members of one class into another class
original.explanation: Class abstraction separates class implementation from the use of the class; the creator describes how to use it and the user needs no implementation details.
option_explanations: Public fields expose the implementation, the opposite of abstraction.
Correct: abstraction hides the implementation behind a description of use.
That describes an abstract class, a different feature.
Copying members is code duplication, not abstraction.

versions.question: A programmer calls the methods of a library class without ever reading its source code. Which principle makes this possible?
versions.explanation: Users work from the class description; implementation details are hidden.
option_explanations: Overloading is several methods sharing one name.
Static binding is about when a call is resolved.
Correct: the user relies on the description, not the code.

versions.question: The lecture compares using a class to using a PC without knowing how it works inside. Which statement matches this comparison?
options: Clients need the class's description, not its internals
Clients must read the source before they use a class
Clients should change a class's private fields directly
Clients decide how each method is implemented
versions.explanation: The implementation is a black box encapsulated and hidden from the user.
option_explanations: Correct: a user only needs to know how to use it.
The point is that reading the source is unnecessary.
Private fields are hidden from clients.
The class creator, not the client, writes the implementation.

original.question: What makes up a class contract?
options: Code inside every method and constructor
Names of its private data fields
Signatures of its public methods and public constants
The list of classes that extend it
original.explanation: The contract is the set of public method signatures and public constants; clients use the class through it.
option_explanations: Method bodies are the hidden implementation.
Private fields are not visible to clients.
Correct: the contract is the public signatures and constants.
Subclasses are not part of the contract.

versions.question: Client code depends on which part of a class?
options: Its private fields and helper methods
Its method bodies and local variables
Its public method signatures and constants
versions.explanation: Clients use the class through its contract, the public signatures and constants.
option_explanations: Private members are hidden from clients.
Comments and names are not the contract.

versions.question: Which change to the Course class breaks its contract for existing client code?
options: Renaming the public method addStudent to add
Replacing the students array with another data structure
versions.explanation: Changing a public signature changes the contract; internal changes do not affect clients.
option_explanations: Correct: clients calling addStudent would no longer compile.
Internals may change if public methods stay the same.
Method bodies are not part of the contract.
Private fields are not visible to clients.

original.question: The Course class stores students in an array. Its author later switches to another data structure but keeps the public methods unchanged. What happens to programs that use Course?
options: They must change every call to addStudent
They must declare the new data structure
They fail until the fields are made public
They keep working without any changes
original.explanation: Because the contract of public methods is unchanged, the implementation can change freely.
option_explanations: Clients never see the data structure.
Fields stay private; clients use methods.
Correct: clients only depend on the public methods.

versions.question: A client program uses Course through addStudent, dropStudent and getNumberOfStudents. The internal array is replaced by a different structure with the same public methods. Which statement is true?
options: The client code must be rewritten to match
The client code can stay exactly as it is
The client must now access the structure itself
The client must call new helper methods
versions.explanation: Encapsulation hides the structure; only the contract matters to the client.
option_explanations: No new methods were added to the contract.

versions.question: Why can the author of Course choose any data structure to hold the students?
options: The structure is hidden behind the public methods
Arrays are the only structure Java allows
The structure is chosen by each client
Fields of a class are always public
versions.explanation: Encapsulation hides implementation details from the user as long as the contract is kept.
option_explanations: Correct: clients only see the public methods.
Java allows many data structures, so an array is not forced.
Fields are private by good design.

original.question: In the Loan UML diagram, which entry is a private data field?
original.explanation: In UML a minus sign marks a private member and a plus sign a public member; fields are written name: type.
option_explanations: Correct: minus means private and name: type means a field.

versions.question: In UML, what does the minus sign in front of -numberOfYears: int indicate?
options: The field starts at a negative value
versions.explanation: A leading minus in a UML class diagram means private; plus means public.
option_explanations: Static members are underlined in UML, not marked with a minus.
Read-only is not shown by the sign.
The sign says nothing about the value.

versions.question: Which UML line declares a public method that returns a String?
versions.explanation: Plus means public; the type after the colon of a method is its return type.
option_explanations: This is a private data field.
This returns void and takes a String.
Correct: public, with String as return type.

original.question: In the UML member +setLoanAmount(loanAmount: double): void, what is the return type?
original.explanation: The type after the colon that follows the parentheses is the return type; parameters are written name: type inside them.
option_explanations: Correct: the colon after the parentheses gives the return type.

versions.question: In the UML member +getBMI(): double, what does double describe?
options: The type of its only parameter
The type of a private field
The return type of the method
versions.explanation: The part after the closing parenthesis and colon is the return type.
option_explanations: There are no parameters in the parentheses.
It is a method, not a field.
Correct: double is what the method returns.

versions.question: Which pair is correct for the UML member +push(value: int): int?
options: Takes an int parameter and returns an int
Takes no parameter and returns an int
Takes an int parameter and returns void
Takes an int and is private
versions.explanation: Inside the parentheses are name: type parameters; after them comes the return type.
option_explanations: Correct: value: int is the parameter and : int the return type.
The return type shown is int, not void.

original.explanation: The no-arg constructor leaves the defaults, and the setter changes only the amount.
option_explanations: a does not take b's years.
Correct: a keeps 1 year; its amount becomes 25000 / 5.

versions.explanation: y comes from the default constructor (1 year) and its amount is set to twice x's amount.
option_explanations: y does not copy x's years.
Correct: default years is 1; amount set to 8000 * 2.

versions.explanation: The default constructor uses 2.5; the other uses the passed value as a double.
option_explanations: p is not changed by q's construction.

original.question: How do procedural programming and object-oriented programming treat data and the operations on it?
options: Procedural bundles them in objects; OO keeps them separate
Both keep them separate but OO uses more methods
Both bundle them but procedural uses classes
Procedural keeps them separate; OO bundles them in objects
original.explanation: In procedural programming data are passed to methods; in OO an object holds both data and operations.
option_explanations: Procedural programming has no classes of objects.
Correct: data are passed to methods vs objects own both.

versions.question: A method must be given the weight and height as arguments each time. Which paradigm does this describe?
versions.explanation: In procedural programming the data are separate from the operations and must be passed to them.
option_explanations: In OO the object already holds its data.
Correct: data and operations are separate, so data must be passed.

versions.question: In which style does a BMI object calculate its own status from its own fields?
options: Object-oriented, but with data in separate classes
versions.explanation: OO objects are associated with both data and operations, so no data need to be passed.
option_explanations: Correct: the object has its fields and its methods.
Procedural does not tie data to operations.
OO objects keep their own data.

original.explanation: The three-argument constructor passes the default age 20 on to the four-argument one.

versions.explanation: The first call passes age 31; the second uses the default 20.
option_explanations: The second object uses the default.

versions.question: BMI has constructors BMI(name, age, weight, height) and BMI(name, weight, height), where the second uses default age 20. Which statement creates a person with the default age?
versions.explanation: Leaving out the age selects the three-argument constructor.
option_explanations: That sets age to 140 through the first constructor.
The argument order does not match any constructor.
Correct: name, weight, height matches the second constructor.

original.question: Which list gives the four common relationships among classes?
original.explanation: The four relationships are association, aggregation, composition and inheritance.
option_explanations: Polymorphism is not a class relationship.
Correct: the four named in the lecture.

versions.question: Which of these is not one of the four class relationships in the lecture?
versions.explanation: The relationships are association, aggregation, composition and inheritance.
option_explanations: Correct: overriding is a method feature, not a class relationship.

versions.question: Fill in the missing term: association, aggregation, ____, inheritance.
versions.explanation: Composition is the third class relationship.

original.question: What is an association between two classes?
options: A relationship where one class extends the other
A relationship where one object owns the other's lifetime
A general binary relationship describing an activity between them
A field that stores an array of objects
original.explanation: Association is a general binary relationship that describes an activity between two classes.
option_explanations: Correct: it is general and describes an activity.
That is just one way to code a relationship.

versions.question: A student taking a course is an example of which relationship?
versions.explanation: Student and Course are linked by an activity, taking, which is an association.
option_explanations: A student is not a kind of course.
A course is not owned by the student.
Correct: an activity between two classes.

versions.question: Which pair is an association as described in the lecture?
options: A faculty member and the course taught
A student and the student's name
versions.explanation: Teaching is an activity linking Faculty and Course.
option_explanations: Correct: teaching is an activity between two classes.
A name is held in a data field of Student; that is aggregation or composition, not an activity.

original.question: How is an association drawn in a UML class diagram?
options: A solid line ending in a hollow triangle
A line with a filled diamond at one end
A line with an empty diamond at one end
A solid line with an optional label and direction triangle
original.explanation: An association is a solid line between two classes, optionally with a label and a small black triangle for direction.
option_explanations: Correct: a plain solid line, label and triangle optional.

versions.question: On an association line, what does the small black triangle show?
options: Which way the relationship is read
That one class extends the other
versions.explanation: The triangle gives the direction of the relationship, such as a student takes a course.
option_explanations: Correct: it shows the reading direction.
Inheritance uses a hollow triangle arrow.

versions.question: The words Take and Teach on association lines are what?
options: Names of the fields in the classes
versions.explanation: Labels are optional descriptions of the activity.
option_explanations: Field names are not the labels.

original.question: Which statement distinguishes composition from aggregation?
options: In composition the part may outlive its owner
In aggregation the owner destroys the part
In composition the part has no purpose without its owner
Composition is drawn with an empty diamond
original.explanation: Composition means A owns B and B has no purpose without A; in aggregation B exists independently.
option_explanations: Correct: the part depends on the owner.

versions.question: When a text editor closes, its Buffer is destroyed but the File it used is not. How are the relationships classified?
options: Buffer is aggregation, File is composition
Buffer is composition, File is aggregation
versions.explanation: A part that disappears with its owner is composition; one that survives is aggregation.
option_explanations: Correct: Buffer depends on the editor, File does not.
The Buffer is destroyed with the editor.

versions.question: When a Company ceases to do business its Accounts cease to exist but its People continue to exist. How are the relationships classified?
options: Accounts are aggregation, People are composition
Accounts are composition, People are aggregation
versions.explanation: Accounts depend on the company; People exist independently.
option_explanations: Correct: accounts vanish with the company, people do not.

original.question: Aggregation models which kind of relationship?
original.explanation: Aggregation is a has-a relationship that represents ownership between two objects.
option_explanations: Correct: an object has another object.
That is not a class relationship.

versions.question: Composition is best described as which of the following?
versions.explanation: Composition is a special case of the aggregation relationship, with stronger ownership.
option_explanations: Correct: it is a stronger form of aggregation.

versions.question: Which phrase correctly describes the relationship between a Student and an Address field?
versions.explanation: A data field of another class is a has-a relationship.

original.question: In UML, a filled diamond attached to the aggregating class denotes which relationship?
original.explanation: A filled diamond marks composition; an empty diamond marks aggregation.

versions.question: A UML line between Student and Address has an empty diamond at the Student end. What does it show?
versions.explanation: An empty diamond at the aggregating class denotes aggregation.

versions.question: Which UML symbol marks composition?
options: A filled diamond at the owner's end
An empty diamond at the owner's end
A hollow triangle at the parent's end
A plain line with a direction triangle
versions.explanation: The filled diamond is attached to the aggregating (owner) class.
option_explanations: Correct: filled diamond at the owner.

original.question: In the code, an aggregation relationship is represented how?
options: A field of the aggregating class inside the other class
The aggregating class extending the other class
A static method in the other class
A data field of the other class inside the aggregating class
original.explanation: The aggregating class (Student) holds data fields whose types are the aggregated classes (Name, Address).
option_explanations: That reverses who holds the field.
A static method is not a relationship.
Correct: Student declares fields of type Name and Address.

versions.explanation: A reference data field that is not initialised holds null.
option_explanations: Correct: an unset object field is null.

versions.explanation: An uninitialised reference field is null, so the comparison is true.
option_explanations: name is null, not an object.
The comparison gives a boolean, not null.

original.question: A person has one supervisor who is also a Person. Which field inside Person models this?
original.explanation: Aggregation may exist between objects of the same class: the data field's type is the class itself.
option_explanations: Supervisor is not a class here.
extends is not valid in a field.
Correct: a field of the class's own type.
A static field would be shared by all persons.

versions.question: A person can have several supervisors, all of class Person. Which field fits?
versions.explanation: With multiplicity m the aggregating class holds an array of its own type.
option_explanations: Correct: an array holds many supervisors.
That is not valid Java syntax.
An int cannot hold Person objects.

versions.explanation: x never received a supervisor, so its supervisor field is null; x.getSupervisor() == null is true.
option_explanations: y's supervisor was set, not x's.
Correct: x's supervisor was never set.

original.question: In a UML diagram Student 1..3 --- 1 Address, what does 1..3 beside Student mean?
options: A student has one to three addresses
An address can be shared by one to three students
A student can take one to three courses
Three students must share one name
original.explanation: The multiplicity next to a class says how many of its objects take part: an address may be shared by up to three students.
option_explanations: The 1 beside Address says one address per student.
Courses are not in this diagram.
Names are not in this diagram.

versions.question: In the diagram Student 1..3 --- 1 Address, what does the 1 beside Address mean?
options: Each address has exactly one student
A student has between one and three addresses
The address is shared by exactly one name
Each student has exactly one address
versions.explanation: The number beside a class says how many of that class's objects a related object has.
option_explanations: That would be a 1 beside Student.
Names are not in this diagram.
Correct: every student has a single address.

versions.question: In the Person-supervisor diagram, what does the multiplicity m on the supervisor end allow?
options: A person can have many supervisors, held in an array
A supervisor can have only one person
A person can have exactly one supervisor in a single field
A supervisor must be a subclass of Person
versions.explanation: Using m lets one Person have several supervisors, so the aggregating class holds an array of Person.
option_explanations: Correct: m means many supervisors per person.
m is not limited to one.
One field holds a single supervisor.

original.question: In the summary diagram Apple is joined to Fruit by a line ending in a hollow triangle at Fruit. Which relationship is shown?
original.explanation: A hollow triangle arrow points to the superclass and shows inheritance (is-a).

versions.question: A UML line ends in a hollow triangle at class Shape. What does this say about the other class?
options: It takes part in an activity with Shape
versions.explanation: A hollow triangle at the superclass marks inheritance.
option_explanations: That would be a diamond at Shape.
Correct: the triangle marks the superclass.

versions.question: Which relationship is Apple to Fruit?
versions.explanation: Inheritance is the is-a relationship: an Apple is a Fruit.
option_explanations: Correct: an Apple is a Fruit.

original.question: Which code matches a two-way association between Teacher and Course?
options: Course is declared as an array of Teacher
Each class is declared inside the other
Teacher has a Course field and Course has a Teacher field
original.explanation: An association is coded with fields of the other class, here one in each class.
option_explanations: An array of Teacher is not an association.
Nested declaration is not an association.
Correct: each class refers to the other.

versions.question: Class Account has a field of type Company and class Company has a field of type Account. Which relationship does this code show?
versions.explanation: Each class holds a reference to the other, a two-way association.
option_explanations: Correct: both classes refer to each other.

versions.question: In the summary, aggregation of Company over Employee is coded how?
options: Company has a field of type Employee
Employee has a field of type Company
versions.explanation: The aggregating class holds a data field of the aggregated class.
option_explanations: Correct: Company holds an Employee field.

original.question: A House creates its Room objects and the rooms have no purpose outside that house. Which relationship is this?
original.explanation: A part that has no purpose without its owner is composition.
option_explanations: Correct: the rooms depend on the house.
A room is not a kind of house.

versions.question: A Team holds Player objects, and players can leave and exist on their own. Which relationship is this?
versions.explanation: Parts that exist independently of the owner give aggregation.
option_explanations: Composition parts depend on the owner.
A player is not a kind of team.

versions.question: A Doctor treats a Patient, with neither owning the other. Which relationship is this?
versions.explanation: Treating is an activity between two classes, with no ownership.
option_explanations: A patient is not a kind of doctor.

original.explanation: After dropping Bob, Cy shifts into index 1 and the count falls to 2.
option_explanations: Correct: count is 2 and s[1] is now Cy.

versions.explanation: Dropping the first student shifts Ed to index 0 and reduces the count to 2.
option_explanations: Correct: Ed shifted to index 0; count is 2.

versions.explanation: Zed is not enrolled, so dropStudent changes nothing.

original.question:

versions.question:
Course declares its fields private and offers the public methods addStudent, getStudents, getNumberOfStudents and getCourseName. Which line causes a compile error?

c.courseName = "Math";           // line 2
c.addStudent("Ann");             // line 3
int n = c.getNumberOfStudents(); // line 4

versions.question:
Course declares its fields private and offers the public methods addStudent, getStudents, getNumberOfStudents and getCourseName. Which line causes a compile error?

original.question: In which order does a stack give back its items?
options: In the order of insertion from the bottom
original.explanation: A stack holds data in a last-in, first-out fashion.
option_explanations: Correct: the most recent item leaves first.

versions.question: The values 5, 7 and 9 are pushed onto a stack in that order. Which value does the next pop return?
versions.explanation: The last value pushed is the first popped.
option_explanations: 5 would come out of a queue.

versions.question: Which real-world situation behaves like a stack?
options: A pile of plates where you take the top one
A line of people waiting at a ticket window
A numbered list read from the first entry
A row of cars passing a toll booth
versions.explanation: Taking the most recently placed item first is last-in, first-out.
option_explanations: Correct: the last plate placed is taken first.

peek reads the top; pop reads and removes it
peek reads the bottom; pop removes the top
peek removes every element; pop removes one

original.question: What default capacity does the no-argument constructor of StackOfIntegers give?

versions.question: Which statement creates an empty StackOfIntegers with capacity 50?

versions.question: The UML for StackOfIntegers lists +StackOfIntegers(capacity: int). What does it do?
options: Constructs an empty stack with the given capacity
Sets the size field to capacity
versions.explanation: The parameter is the capacity of the underlying array; the new stack has no elements.
option_explanations: Correct: an empty stack of that capacity.

original.question: Which StackOfIntegers method returns true when no integers are stored?
original.explanation: empty() has return type boolean; the UML says it returns true if the stack is empty.

versions.question: Which StackOfIntegers method returns the number of integers stored?

versions.question: Which StackOfIntegers method has a boolean return type?
versions.explanation: empty() is the only boolean method in the UML.
option_explanations: Correct: it returns true or false.

original.question: Which wrapper class corresponds to the primitive type char?
original.explanation: The wrappers are Boolean, Character, Short, Byte, Integer, Long, Float and Double.
option_explanations: Char is not a Java class.

versions.question: Which wrapper class corresponds to int?
versions.explanation: int is wrapped by Integer; most wrappers just capitalise the primitive name, except int and char.

versions.question: Which primitive and wrapper pair is matched correctly?
versions.explanation: Each primitive has its own wrapper class: boolean-Boolean, float-Float, char-Character, long-Long.

original.question: When are wrapper classes used?
options: When a primitive must run faster
When a value must be changed after creation
When a number needs more than 64 bits
When an object representation of a primitive is required
original.explanation: Wrapper classes give an object form of a primitive value; their instances are immutable.
option_explanations: Correct: they provide an object form of a primitive.

versions.question: Which declaration needs a wrapper class instead of a primitive type?

versions.question: A method parameter must be an object, but you hold a double value. Which type do you use?
versions.explanation: Double is the wrapper that provides the object form of a double.

original.question: What happens when `Integer count = new Integer();` is compiled?

versions.question: What happens when `Double price = new Double();` is compiled?
options: It compiles and price is null
It throws an exception when run

options: The smallest double with no fraction
original.explanation: For Float and Double, MIN_VALUE is the smallest positive value, not the most negative.

versions.question:

Name 1 ----(filled diamond)---- 1 Student    (composition: filled diamond attached to the aggregating class Student)
